author: Earwig Foundation
title: We adhere to the following investment philosophy: To build a
text:
We adhere to the following investment philosophy: To build an intentional portfolio of great companies trading at good prices to hold forever. We recently ran Cirrus Logic (NASDAQ: CRUS ) through our screening process and the results were intriguing. 
The Business and Industry Cirrus Logic is a leader in high-performance, low-power integrated circuits for audio and voice signal processing applications. Cirrus Logic’s products span the entire audio signal chain, from capture to playback, providing innovative components for the world’s top smartphones, tablets, digital headsets, wearables and emerging smart home applications.
CRUS is a mid-cap technology company that has grown significantly since going public in 1989. Its recent run of success has been tied to the success of the smartphone market and consumer demand for high-quality audio and voice components in their phones. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is a large customer of CRUS technology and the biggest source of company revenues. Much of CRUS' past success and future performance will be dependent on Apple's new product success and their willingness to continue to use CRUS circuits.
Is CRUS a "Great Company?" To screen possible portfolio additions in the "great company" category we focus on six easy-to-find and understandable metrics:
1. 10-year EPS growth (no non-recurring items)
2. 10-year revenue growth
Revenue growth and EPS growth over the long term are fundamental to growing the value of a company. If customers are willing to buy more and more of a company's products at higher prices each year (increasing revenue) that's clearly a positive sign for the quality of the business. But unless that revenue growth is paired with EPS growth, we can be a bit skeptical about management decisions. For instance, are they ramming products down their customer's throats through enormous marketing spend, or are they just plain inefficient in managing expenses or issuing shares? 
CRUS 10-year revenue growth rate of 27.5% coupled with their nearly 29% EPS growth rate show that not only is CRUS selling quite a bit more each year, but they are managing this growth by responsibly growing expenses. CEO Jason Rhode has been leading CRUS since 2007, the beginning of this impressive 10-year run. We love it when the CEO leading the future has been the one driving impressive past results.
3. Net margin
4. Net margin expansion?
We like investing in companies with relatively high net margins. The higher the net margin (particularly over a long term), the larger the moat or competitive advantage that this company might have. Successful businesses bread imitators. As Jeff Bezos likes to say "your margin is my opportunity." If a high-margin business finds itself suddenly facing stiff competition, it will likely need to lower its prices to retain business. But the best businesses to invest in have a significant moat around their business protecting it from the competition. This moat may be in the form of patents, brand power or government regulation. A high net margin over the long term is a great indicator of a moat. An even better result is if that net margin is expanding. This is an indicator that management has the power to price their products higher without losing customers or incurring significant new expenditures. 
Cirrus Logic's net margin has been a bit lumpy over the last 10 years as the revenue growth and expense growth has not always matched up on the same annual income statement. But its current 17.1% is much better than the S&P 500 margin at 9.29% or the industry average for CRUS's competitors with a similar market cap. Their net margin over the last 10 years also has grown from 15.3% in 2008 to 17.1% today.
5. Return on Equity
We love the return metrics when it comes to analyzing management and business quality. As long-term holders, we want to own businesses that are compounding our returns year after year even when considering retained earnings. ROE is an easy to calculate metric that does a pretty good job of analyzing management's success at compounding returns. 
Cirrus Logic's current ROE of 24.47% bests even its respectable 18.85% 13-year median. And with no debt, we are not concerned that the company's return is built on the back of a risky balance sheet.
6. Business predictability rank
The business predictability rank is a star-rating assigned by the value investing Website Guru Focus. They rank the predictability based on the consistency of revenue per share and EBITDA over a 10-year period, which typically encompasses a full business cycle (both ups and downs). This is a good metric for predicting the reliability of future results based on historical performance. The more predictable the company's revenues and EBITDA, the more likely that future results will mirror historical results. 
This is one metric that does not score very well for CRUS. CRUS ranked a one star for business predictability. That is the lowest score. But Guru Focus punishes companies harshly for a negative EBITDA score. CRUS had a negative EBITDA in 2008 but has been all positive since. Hence the one-star rating. It should be noted that 76% of GURU Focus tested companies had a one-star rating. That shows just how challenging it is for a business to post consistent revenues and EBITDA during both up and down economic cycles. 
Is CRUS Trading at a Good Price? Once we have screened CRUS against the "Great Business" metrics, we take a look at valuation by screening against the following five metrics:
1. PE
2. Median 13 year PE
We love to consider a company's current valuation in relation to its historical valuation. We feel this is a better indicator of value than comparing it against the broader market or competitors. When the current PE is below the median 13 year PE, we get excited. Currently, the CRUS PE of 12.25 is 33% below its 13-year median of 18.42 . That could indicate 33% upside from here before you even consider the company's ability to grow and compound returns.
3. PEG
Price to earnings divided by the five-year average EBITDA growth rate gives us the PEG ratio. For this metric, the lower the PEG, the better the potential valuation. We rarely find great companies with PEG ratios below one. CRUS' current peg is very attractive at .54. The market loves growth. Therefore, when we see a PEG ratio this low, it typically means the market is skeptical that the historic growth of this company is likely to continue. We'll dig into that assumption later.
4. Forward Rate of Return
The Forward Rate of Return is a metric created by Guru Focus based on an analysis of the investing style of the former portfolio manager of Selected American Shares mutual fund, Donald Yachtman. Donald's investing philosophy mirrors our own, so we love to look at this simple metric as a valuation screener. This metric divides the seven-year average normalized free cash flow by the sum of the share price and the earnings growth. The result of this calculation is a percentage which can be thought of as the return that investors buying the stock today can expect from it in the future.
CRUS' current forward rate of return is 23.7%, which if accurate would give today's investors quite a nice rate of compounding returns.
5. Margin of Safety
The Margin of Safety is the percent difference between a company's intrinsic value (using discount cash flow calculation) and its current market price. This is not our favorite metric because the results rely so heavily on projecting a future EPS growth rate. Any slight alteration of that growth rate can have quite significant results on the intrinsic value calculation and the resulting margin of safety. But by measuring valuation based on five different valuation metrics, we are not overly reliant on any one of them. So DCF calculated margin of safety is just one more tool for our toolkit. 
Using CRUS' 10-year historical EPS growth rate of 29% results in an intrinsic value calculation of $210 per share. Comparing that result to the current share price of $51.65 results in a 75% margin of safety . This is another amazing result for one of our valuation metrics. 
Why Is This "Great" Company Trading at such a "Good" Price? CRUS' results in our "Great" company and "Good" price screeners as outstanding. It is not often that you can find such a profitable growing company trading at such an attractive valuation - particularly in such a mature stage of a bull market. So why is the market so heavily discounting CRUS?
We were able to find two possible reasons why CRUS stock is not trading at a higher valuation:
1. Revenue growth is slowing. In the Q2 2018 shareholder letter , which accompanied financial results, the company disclosed a 1% year-over-year decline in revenue. "The slight decline in revenue on a year-over-year basis reflects, as previously disclosed, the sale of a lower ASP component at a key Android OEM and ASP reductions on certain other portable audio products, which was offset partially by an increase in volumes on a number of portable audio components." Lower revenue and lower average selling prices on products are exactly the opposite of what we like to see. Earlier we lauded CRUS' high historic revenue and net margin growth rates. Is it possible those amazing growth rates are in the rear-view mirror never to be seen again? Clearly, that's what the market thinks. It is also possible that these lower growth rates and margins are a bit of a short-term issue, with the long-term prospect for future growth still strong. One thing is for certain when growth rates shift from positive to negative, the market is not happy and stock prices suffer.
2. Heavy reliance on one customer (Apple). The major anchor currently weighing down shares is Cirrus' heavy reliance on Apple for the majority of its revenue (79% in 2017) . The risk of investing in a company with such a heavy reliance on one customer is that customer may eventually choose to purchase these products from another vendor or change the design in such a way to make CRUS products unnecessary. Either of these decisions, which fall outside of CRUS control, would have a significant negative impact on CRUS' revenue. Indeed this would be a game changer. Fellow Seeking Alpha author Rational Techne, in his article Cirrus Logic: A Potential Black Swan , did a fine job of highlighting the downside of this risk.
But the converse also is a possibility, and perhaps a more likely one. Isn't it possible in a world where all the smartphone manufacturers are trying to copy Apple, that CRUS' sales to other OEMs are likely to increase? Isn't it also pretty exciting to have such a tight partnership with the world's leading technology company? Are we being a bit short sighted and overly fearful by assuming that Apple iPhone sales are the only future source of revenue for CRUS? The connected home and connected auto are in the early stages of growth and development and both these emerging markets will rely heavily on the type of high-quality audio chips that CRUS makes. CRUS is projecting to spend over $130 million in research and development in the December quarter. That spend eclipses their entire quarterly operating expenses in Q2. CRUS is clearly investing in the future and is likely doing it hand in hand with its biggest customer. We just can't see exactly what that future looks like yet, but isn't that always the case in investing? 
Conclusion: Buy or Pass? We think CRUS' impressive long-term results and attractive valuation warrant an entry at these prices. This is not a risk-free investment, but they never are.
